messages.subject_clean: [distance-sampling] Distance in R - comparison of pooled CDS, stratified CDS and MCDS
messages.body_plain:
Tom

You ask a series of good questions.  I'll not try to answer all of them, but make a few comments:

Q1 - your are correct in your interpretations; by binning data at time of data collection, you limit the types of analyses you can conduct.  Degrees of freedom available for a chi-square goodness of fit test is (number of distance bins) - 1 - (parameters in model).  You are left with assessment of fit based upon visual assessment of the fitted pdf to the histogram.  You can at least say something about the agreement between your data and the fitted values.

Q2 - I haven't looked at this for a while so I don't know the details of the stratified analysis of Marques et al. (2007).  Fortunately, if you have downloaded the GUI version of Distance (as opposed to the R package), you have the analyses performed by Marques et al. (2007) in a project called "Amakihi.dst"--you can pour over the details yourself.

Q3 - see Q2

Q4 - Recognise the covariates used in Marques et al. (2007) were observer and minutes after sunrise.  Both have fairly obvious relationships to detectability; it is less obvious that forest age or site might be influential in detectability; but it is difficult to speak in generalities about your particular study.  One comment I would mention regarding the results you provide is the really small P_a estimates of nearly all of your models.  The estimates you show suggest the detection function is falling away very rapidly and that for each bird you detect in your plots, there are 10 more you don't detect.  That's going to make for a difficult inference task.

messages.body_plain:
Don

I believe the answer is simpler than you are trying to make it.  Section 1.5 of Buckland et al. (2015) defines the *detection function g(x)* as "the probability of detecting an animal that is at distance x from the transect (0 < x < w)".  Using plot.ds() will show you the fitted detection function and you can interpret the values from that curve as you describe.  For a value x satisfying g(x)=0.75, that x corresponds to the distance at which 25% of the objects located at that distance are missed.

The computation of ESW uses what we denote as P_a multiplied by w.  The quantity P_a is the probability that an object is detected, given it is *anywhere* up to distance w from the transect.

Hello Eric,

Many thanks for your responses, particularly in terms of Q1, and how to proceed when unable to conduct a goodness-of-fit test.

In reference to Q's 2 & 3, I contacted Tiago Marques about this. He very kindly offered some advice, which I will share here in case anyone here has a similar situation. The program Distance (as opposed to Distance for R) automatically calculates a total AIC value for stratified analyses (i.e. a single value across all strata). To obtain equivalent values when using the R package, one can sum the AIC for each stratum-specific model with the AIC values for the corresponding models in the other strata. This combined value can then be compared with the pooled analyses in AIC model selection.

In regards to Q4, I absolutely agree Eric, there isn't a huge reason to expect habitat age will affect detectability, but for my study it is important to be able to discount that possibility.

Thanks again,
Tom

messages.body_plain:
Road surveys:

The purpose of a survey design is the create a *random* sample of your study area such that you can have confidence in the assumption that the places you sampled with your transects are representative of the area to which you wish to make inference.  By definition, roads are not placed randomly on the landscape, hence it is contradictory to "design" a road survey.  That is the reason you are unable to find information regarding this subject.  It would be best to not use roads for your sampling.

Animals know where roads are located and the either avoid roads or are attracted to them; in either case, this interferes with your ability to make sound inference from surveys that are road based.

A better strategy is to define the area about which you wish to make inference, then use the Distance software or some other random process to place transects into that area.  It is best to have more short transects than a small number of short transects.  You need replicates across the study area to have more confidence in your results.

Feel free to ask additional questions.

Hi Chris, list

The only way I can think of being able to combine the two sets of information for full efficiency is by writing down a bespoke likelihood made up of two components, one with binned data, the other with exact distances, but which share the parameters of interest. That will involve necessarily a bit of coding - might be a nice student project, say.

>From a pragmatic point of view, in Distance you could simply fit a detection function to the data from island B, and then get the probability of detection (P) and the corresponding standard error (se) from the Distance analysis. Then you run an analysis of the data of Island A only, force Distance to use a Uniform detection function with no adjustments, and then add a multiplier that is the P with the corresponding se. In this way, distance will do all the correct calculations for you and the reported results will be the same as if you had used the data from B to get the detection probability and the data from A for the encounter rate, which I believe is what you want (Is the maximum detection distance in both islands about the same?).

Note that the fact that you say that when you bin the data of island B and pool with island A data you don't get a "good detection model" does not fill me with confidence. The reliability of any of the analysis options noted above depends on the detection process being the same (shared parameters across the likelihoods or same P across islands), and a no "good detection model" might be an indication that this is not necessarily true.

Hope this helps,

messages.body_plain:
Sara

Survey design is important for ensuring the transects you sample are representative of the area you wish to study.  The key element in survey design is the element of randomness.  We cannot, with our eyes, decide where to place our transects so as to be representative of the study area.

The purpose of the survey design engine is to allow you to define your study region and a few other details, then the software will examine designs within that region consistent with your design specifications.  Having examined the characteristics of the design, you can have the software produce a single realisation of that design that, as you say, specifies the locations of your transects.

It does not make sense to "design" your survey after the sampling has been conducted.

The most delicate part of the question you ask is here "do the transects in the most appropriate way on the beach".  From a statistical perspective "most appropriate way" is defined as *most representative* i.e. being comfortable with the idea that where you did sample resembles where you did not sample.

As we discussed in our earlier correspondence, it is better to have many short transects than few short transects.  The design you provide has but 5 transects, it would be better to have 20 transects.  Hence instead of 5 transects of length 20m, consider having 20 transects of length 5m.
